title: Deep river
hookLine: a spiritual of longing to cross over into campground
tomorrow: pray without ceasing. literally nonstop, or something else?
last: SOMETIMES IT CAUSES ME TO TREMBLE.

lines: A HOME SONG WITH NO HOUSE IN IT.
cards: Most songs about going home name something: a street, a porch light, a face at the door. This one names none of that.
Deep River is a spiritual, short and slow, and nearly all it sings is this: “Deep river, my home is over Jordan.” Deep river, Lord, I want to cross over into campground. No house.
No description of home at all. Just a river in the way, and on the far side, of all things, a campground. Why a river?
And why would anyone long for a campground?

teach.b: Clue one: the river has a name, and the Bible already has a crossing there. In the book of Joshua, Israel has come through the wilderness to the edge of the promised land.
The priests carry the ark into the Jordan, and the King James says the waters “stood and rose up upon an heap,” and “the people passed over right against Jericho.”
That's the one to tell a friend tonight: a river that stood up so a whole people could walk home.
Clue two: the far bank holds more than one home. Some hear heaven in it: the Jordan as death, the other side as rest with God.
Tradition also remembers a nearer longing; for people held in slavery, crossing over could mean freedom. The song doesn't choose between them. It holds both.
Clue three: campground. Some readers hear the camp meetings, outdoor gatherings for singing and prayer. Others hear the camp of Israel, pitched on the far side of the river.
Either way, it solves the puzzle.
A camp is where people are gathered. Home, in this song, isn't a house you arrive at alone. It's a crowd that's waiting for you.
And the song is honest about the cost.
It never pretends the river is shallow.
The depth is right there in the title.

how: Choirs and soloists sing Deep River in church services and in concerts, slowly, letting the long notes carry the longing.

o: a baptism hymn sung at the river's edge
a work song for crossing a flooded field
a spiritual longing to cross the Jordan to home

games.q: what's across the river — tap the pairs.
p: the deep river in the way

s: Deep River describes what home looks like
it never does. just a river, a far bank and a wish to cross.
the Jordan crossing comes from the book of Joshua
the waters rose up upon an heap, and the people passed over right against Jericho.
each spiritual has one secret meaning, a code for escape
some hear freedom, some hear heaven; this song holds both and doesn't choose.

games.q: a friend in choir says campground must be a mistake for 'the promised land.' which reply solves it?
o: a camp is where people gather: camp meetings, or Israel's camp across the Jordan.
it's there for the rhythm; the words of spirituals weren't meant to mean much.
it's a code name for one exact spot on an escape route, nothing more.
games.why: either reading lands in the same place: home is people gathered, not a house you reach alone.

practice: If you can, play a recording of Deep River and let it run; it's slow enough to fill the sit. If not, listen to the nearest steady sound, a fan, rain, traffic, and let it stand in for the river.
Notice where the long notes pull, and what home the pull points to.

wordCard.voice: Deep river. The Jordan in a spiritual: deep, in the way, and home gathered on the far side.

orig.note: the Hebrew name of the Jordan, the river crossed in Joshua and sung in the spiritual.
